open-question.question: Does the draft adopt the 2026-11-19 conversation's new-mission button, which takes a typed goal and opens an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session on it in a terminal, where the person carries the conversation on: as stated, in a refined form, or not at all? The draft's one way to start a mission today is the headless chain of the usage page, its `<goal>` and `<scope>` typed into an input box.
open-question.recommendation: It writes the conversation's own start of a mission into the draft unchanged, the goal typed once and `discuss-mission-goal` proposing the scope from the record, and the "Chain shell session" decision already carries `<goal>` into a line through the session's environment, so free prose in the prompt needs no quoting rule. The headless definition button stays for a goal that is already crisp, at the cost of the two input boxes the draft already has.
open-question.alternative: Adopted as stated: a new-mission button asks for the goal in an input box and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with that goal as the skill's text, where the person carries the conversation on to its proposed goal and `--at` scope and runs `/define-mission-goal` from inside the session; the draft's existing button for the headless `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, its goal and scope typed into input boxes, stays beside it, so the draft names two ways to start a mission. It writes the maintainer's own start of every mission (the transcript's "you click it, you write the goal, ... you will continue the conversation there") into the draft unchanged, gets the scope proposal `discuss-mission-goal` makes from the `record .` read without the person working the scope out, and keeps the one-click headless definition for a goal that is already crisp. The typed goal lands inside the interactive line's quoted prompt, so the quoting rule of "Running a line" now covers free prose of any length, and the draft holds two start buttons whose difference it must explain; the button needs an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` line to exist, which depends on how the sibling question on where interactive lines come from settles, since `docs/ways-of-using.md` holds none.

Adopted as stated for the button itself (goal typed into an input box, an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session opened on it in a terminal, the person defining the mission from inside the session), and it replaces the draft's headless-definition button: the extension offers no button for the `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, `<goal>` and `<scope>` leave the placeholders the interface fills, and that line stays only on the usage page and in a person's own recipes. One way into a mission through the extension, the way the maintainer actually starts one, and the draft loses the scope input box, whose value a person typing it cold is the least placed to choose, since the definition invariant wants it as deep as the core allows and `discuss-mission-goal` is what proposes it. A person with a crisp goal and a known scope must go through a conversation, or paste the headless line by hand, to define a mission the draft's current button defines in one click, and the same quoting exposure for the typed goal and the same condition on the sibling question on interactive line sources apply.

Adopted in a refined form: the new-mission button takes no input and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with no text, the person typing the goal as the conversation's first turn and defining the mission from inside the session; the draft's headless-definition button with its goal and scope input boxes stays beside it. The goal is typed once, into the session that reasons over it, rather than into an input box whose text is then quoted into a command line, so no free prose of the person's passes through the line's quoting at all and the button's line is fixed text with no placeholder at all, while the quick headless definition stays available. It departs from the conversation's stated flow (type the goal, press enter, land in the terminal) by one step, and the person still meets two start buttons; it still needs an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` line from wherever the sibling question on interactive line sources places them.

Adopted in a refined form that also replaces the draft's headless-definition button: the one start button takes no input and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with no text, the person typing the goal there and defining the mission from inside the session, and the extension offers no button for the `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, which stays on the usage page and in a person's own recipes. The smallest interface of the adopting options: one fixed line with no placeholder of the person's own text, no goal or scope input box anywhere in the extension, and no quoting exposure for a mission's start. It removes the one-click definition the draft already has and departs from the stated typed-goal flow at once, so both a crisp-goal start and the transcript's own description are served less directly; it still rests on the sibling question on interactive line sources for its line.

Dropped from the draft for good, listed among the dropped ideas with a one-line reason: the extension gets no new-mission button for `discuss-mission-goal`, its one way to start a mission stays the headless `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line with its two input boxes, and a person who wants the discussion runs `/discuss-mission-goal` by hand in a terminal of their own, as the snippet file's bare slash commands have it today. The draft keeps its present scope with no new interactive line to source, no free-text quoting case added, and nothing more for a first version to build, and starting a mission is rare beside the answering and execution sittings the extension mainly exists for. The step the maintainer begins every mission with stays hand work outside the extension, and the headless button asks for a scope the person must choose without the record read `discuss-mission-goal` makes, which invites the root or another over-wide placement the definition invariant warns against.

open-question.question: How does the extension identify and offer recipes that carry the same `###` heading under different host headings of `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md`? The shipped recipes are recorded as that file's blocks, each recipe read as one `###` heading and its fenced block, while the file repeats its headings under `## Claude Code` and `## Antigravity` (First run, Requirements iteration, the three execution blocks, and Finish mission stand under both), and the draft has a person's own recipe replace a shipped one of the same name.
open-question.recommendation: The "Per-task line composition" decision already has a rule refer to a single-task line by a name of its own, and a button that runs a recipe by a fixed name needs that name to mean exactly one recipe. One flat namespace gives both: the recorded reading rule, a recipe is a `###` heading and its block, holds with no second part, and a flat own recipe file replaces exactly one shipped recipe. The headings are renamed in the same edit that makes the file a shipped document, and the no-repeat check joins the extension's tests in the drift-gate workflow.
open-question.alternative: The snippet file is edited, as part of making it a shipped document, so that every `###` heading is unique across the whole file, each repeated heading naming its host (for example "First run (Antigravity)"), with a check that no heading repeats; a recipe is then identified by its `###` heading alone. The pane offers every shipped recipe grouped under the file's `##` host headings, those headings being display grouping only. A person's own recipe file is a flat list of `###` recipes, an own recipe replacing the shipped one of the same heading and adding a recipe otherwise. One flat namespace serves the shipped file, the own recipe file, and every reference to a recipe by name, so the identity rule is the one the recorded decision already states (a recipe is a `###` heading and its block) and needs no second part. The file's headings get longer and carry the host twice, its uniqueness becomes a rule the maintainer must keep and that needs a check of its own, and a person's own recipe has no way to sit under a host group except by the name it is given.

A recipe is identified by its `##` host heading together with its `###` heading (for example "Claude Code / First run"), and the snippet file keeps its headings as they stand. The pane offers every shipped recipe at once, its buttons grouped under the file's host headings in file order. A person's own recipe file uses the same two-level form, a `##` host heading over `###` recipes: an own recipe replaces the shipped one with the same host heading and the same `###` heading, and is added to that host's group otherwise. Nothing in the snippet file changes and every name is already unique, so the file is read exactly as it is written, and an own recipe replaces exactly one shipped recipe, never another host's line of the same name. Every recipe name, and every reference to one (an own recipe's override, a per-task rule naming a single-task line), carries two parts, an own recipe placed under the wrong or a misspelt host heading silently adds a recipe instead of replacing one, and the pane shows every host's group even to a person who runs only one host; how much this weighs depends on how many hosts the shipped set holds, which the shipped-host-lines question settles.

A recipe is identified by its `##` host heading together with its `###` heading, the snippet file keeping its headings as they stand, and a person's own recipe file uses the same two-level form, replacing the shipped recipe with the same pair and adding to that host otherwise. The pane offers one host group at a time, through a host switch on the pane itself, its choice kept by the editor for the workspace, so only that host's recipes, the ones the file places under it, show as buttons. A person who works in one host sees a short list with one button per recipe name and no duplicate labels, while the file stays unchanged and every override still targets exactly one host's recipe. The extension holds a host choice of its own, a remembered setting beside a recipe set the draft keeps free of host knowledge, and a recipe filed under one host heading but running another host (the Antigravity group's mixed-agent review, its `git log` one-liner) is hidden whenever the other host is selected; the switch is only worth its weight if more than one host ships, which the shipped-host-lines question settles.

A recipe name is its `###` heading, and the pane shows one button per distinct heading; where the same heading stands under more than one `##` host heading (First run, Requirements iteration, the three execution blocks, Finish mission), clicking the button offers those hosts as a choice and runs the chosen host's block. The snippet file keeps its headings as they stand. A person's own recipe file uses the `##` host heading over `###` recipe form, and an own recipe replaces only the shipped variant under the same host and heading, joining the button's host choices otherwise. The pane reads as the person's list of things to do (first run, iterate, execute, finish) with each name once, the host being a choice made at the moment of running, while overrides stay as precise as the qualified form. A shared name presumes the same-named blocks are the same recipe on different hosts, which nothing in the file guarantees (the two execution blocks already differ in model and effort, not only in binary), every run of a shared name costs an extra choice, and the click-time picker is one more interaction the pane must build.

A recipe name is its `###` heading alone, and the pane shows one button per distinct heading, offering the hosts as a choice at click wherever the heading stands under more than one host heading; the snippet file keeps its headings as they stand. A person's own recipe file is a flat list of `###` recipes with no host level, and an own recipe replaces every shipped recipe of the same name, under whichever hosts it stands, leaving one recipe, the person's, behind that button. The own recipe file needs no host structure and a person replaces "First run" once, for every host, which matches a person who keeps one way of running each step. A person cannot replace one host's recipe and keep the other's, so customizing the Claude Code execution block also removes the Antigravity one, and a name collision between the person's file and a shipped recipe they meant to keep replaces several recipes at once.
